title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Ariana Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes summary, known issues, and actionable runbooks used by the Serving Runtime team. It is intended for engineers operating, optimizing, and onboarding new members to the runtime and SRE teams.

Scope

- Runtime architecture: components, data flow, and ownership
- Kernel scheduling: policies, heuristics, and implementation details
- Profiling playbooks: how to collect, interpret, and act on profiles
- Benchmarking suite: standardized workloads, metrics, and CI integration
- Release notes: recent notable changes and performance impact
- Known issues: active bugs and mitigations
- Runbooks & team wiki: operational procedures and links

1) Runtime architecture (high-level)

Summary:
The Serving Runtime (service name: runtime-svc) is a GPU-optimized inference layer that exposes a consistent API to the transport layer (proxy-svc) and to the orchestration layer (orch-svc). Key responsibilities include model loading and caching, KV cache management, request dispatch and continuous batching, quantized execution paths, and health/tracing hooks.

Components and ownership:
- proxy-svc (team: edge) — ingress, TLS termination, rate limiting, per-tenant routing
- runtime-svc (team: serving-runtime) — model execution, batching pipeline, kernel selector
- orch-svc (team: serving-runtime) — placement, autoscaling, capacity-aware routing
- kv-cache (team: serving-runtime) — prefix/KV cache service with LRU eviction and TTL policies
- metrics-agent (team: eng-platform) — collects p99/p50/p95 token latencies, GPU util, memory, queue length
- tracing-sidecar (team: eng-platform) — OpenTelemetry spans and distributed traces

Data flow (request lifecycle):
1. Client -> proxy-svc: authentication, tenant validation, and small pre-checks
2. proxy-svc -> orch-svc: route decision (model variant, region, tier)
3. orch-svc -> runtime-svc: dispatch request to a worker (warmed model shard)
4. runtime-svc: check KV cache -> apply prefix cache if available -> enqueue for batching
5. runtime-svc batching layer: form micro-batches, invoke kernel execution, update KV cache with new KV tokens
6. runtime-svc -> proxy-svc: stream tokens or return final response

SLOs & targets (production):
- 99th percentile token latency (interactive models): < 120ms for small models (sequence <= 256)
- 95th percentile end-to-end request latency (chat endpoint): < 300ms for p95 on tier standard
- GPU utilization target: 65-85% for dedicated pools
- Availability: 99.95% service-level uptime for runtime-svc (see eng-sre SLOs)

2) Kernel scheduling design and heuristics

Goal: maximize throughput and tail-latency predictability while respecting per-tenant latency SLOs and isolation constraints.

Core concepts:
- Kernel selector: picks optimized kernels (attention implementations, fused ops) based on model type, dtype (fp16/int8), sequence length, batch shape, and GPU architecture (A100, H100, etc.).
- Scheduler layers:
  - Admission controller: applies per-tenant rate limit and SLO-aware priority.
  - Coalescing/batching scheduler: dynamic batch formation with max-batch, latency-budget, and shape-awareness.
  - Execution allocator: maps micro-batches to GPU streams and kernels, preferring kernel variants that minimize memory pressure.

Scheduling parameters (defaults):
- max_batch_size: 64 (small models), 16 (long-seq models > 1024)
- latency_budget_ms: 25ms (interactive), 200ms (background/batch)
- coalesce_window_ms: adaptive (default 2-8ms based on qps variability)
- stream_concurrency: 2 per GPU for mixed-precision workloads

Preemption & fairness:
- SLO-aware preemption: requests with high-priority tags (system, health-check, admin) preempt warm low-priority micro-batches. Preemption is soft: scheduler tries to finish near-complete micro-batches to avoid wasted work.
- Isolation via pools: tenant pools use GPU reservations; best-effort tenants scheduled on shared pools with token-based fairness.

Kernel selection policy (example):
- If model dtype == int8 and GPU supports fast-int8-kernel -> use int8-kernel with 2x throughput but perform A/B quality check on first 1k requests after rollout.
- If seq_len <= 256 and attention-type == flash -> prefer flash-attn-optimized kernel.
- For long sequences (>1024) prefer memory-efficient kernels with chunked attention.

3) Profiling playbook (how to capture and act)

When to profile:
- New model onboarding
- After kernel changes or driver updates
- When p95/p99 latency regresses or GPU utilization deviates from expected

Tools & instrumentation:
- perf, nvprof / Nsight systems for low-level GPU traces
- runtime internal tracing: /debug/profile endpoint on runtime-svc (secured) returning async profiles in JSON + flame graphs
- jemalloc + heap profiling (for memory fragmentation cases)
- custom token latency histograms per-model and per-tenant in metrics-agent

Standard profiling steps:
1. Reproduce workload in staging with representative input distribution and seed.
2. Enable detailed tracing: set RUNTIME_PROFILE=on and collect 60s of samples. CLI: curl -s -u admin:token "https://runtime-staging.internal/debug/profile?duration=60s&level=full" > profile.json
3. Generate flame graphs: tools/uftrace -> flame.svg; nvprof -> nvvp files for GPU kernel timelines
4. Key signals to inspect:
   - Kernel duration distribution (per-kernel and per-invocation)
   - Memory peak and allocation hotspots (model load, temporary buffers)
   - Batch formation delays (coalesce wait times)
   - Queue lengths and per-tenant enqueued requests
5. Action items mapping:
   - If kernel duration dominates and alternative kernels exist -> run kernel A/B in staging with metric comparison (latency + correctness).
   - If coalesce wait > latency_budget_ms frequently -> lower coalesce_window_ms or provision additional workers.
   - If memory fragmentation observed -> pin model with preallocated buffers or switch to allocator with aggressive defragmentation.

Profiling checklist (short):
- [ ] Capture 60-300s trace in staging and production canary
- [ ] Correlate traces with metrics (GPU util, p95/p99 latencies)
- [ ] Annotate root cause in ticket and add reproducible steps

4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration

Purpose:
Provide a repeatable set of microbenchmarks and end-to-end benchmarks that measure token/sec, cost-per-token, p50/p95 token latencies, memory usage, and quality regressions for model variants across target hardware.

Benchmark categories:
- Microbenchmarks: single-model kernel perf (vary batch, seq, dtype)
- Throughput benchmarks: sustained token/sec under target concurrency patterns
- Tail-latency benchmarks: synthetic chat bursts and adversarial sequences to measure p95/p99
- E2E scenarios: real prompt distributions derived from production (anonymized)

Bench config (table-like text):
- benchmark_id: "micro-bert-batch-test"
- model: "bert-base-quantized-v2"
- hw_targets: ["a100-40gb","h100-80gb"]
- batch_shapes_tested: ["1x128","8x128","16x128","32x128"]
- metrics_collected: ["tokens_per_sec","p50_token_ms","p95_token_ms","gpu_mem_peak","cost_usd_per_1M_tokens"]

CI integration:
- nightly-bench pipeline runs full-suite on a single A100 staging cluster and uploads reports to artifacts (s3://redwood-bench-reports/<date>/).
- PR gate: lightweight microbench run (selected kernels + smoke) triggered on any change to runtime-svc, kernel selector, or CI images. Thresholds defined in bench-thresholds.yaml (see repo: infra/bench/bench-thresholds.yaml).
- Auto-notifications: bench regression triggers a Slack alert in #runtime-bench-alerts and creates a GitHub issue with attached diff report.

Interpreting results:
- Compare to baseline (last successful nightly). Use token/sec delta > 5% or p95 increase > 8% as automatic regression criteria for blocking release.
- Quality regressions (top-1 token differences) tracked by rouge-like scripts in bench-quality/ and flagged for manual triage.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)

2029-06-20 | runtime-svc v4.12.0 (production rollout)
- Feature: int8 kernel pipeline enabled for selected quantized models. Default off for new models; enabled for models tagged quantized-v2 after canary.
- Perf: adaptive coalesce window improved p95 by 12% on small models at 10-50 qps.
- Fix: memory leak in model loader resolved (root cause: temporary buffer not freed on partial load failure).
- Impact: observed production avg GPU mem reduction of ~8% in dedicated pools.

2029-05-03 | runtime-svc v4.11.2 (hotfix)
- Fix: scheduler race causing duplicated KV-cache entries under heavy load.
- Mitigation: temporarily increased coalesce_window_ms in shared pools to reduce race frequency.

Upgrade & rollout guidance:
1. Canary (5% traffic) for 24 hours, collect microbench + e2e traces
2. If no regressions, increment to 25% for 12 hours and validate p95/p99, GPU util
3. Full rollout in 6-hour windows across regions with emergency rollback tag preserved

6) Known issues (active)

- ISSUE-2029-141: intermittent p99 spikes for long-sequence models when H100 memory compaction runs concurrently. Workaround: schedule compaction during low-traffic windows or use reserved pool nodes with compaction disabled. Owner: Marcus Lee.
- ISSUE-2029-138: rare nvlink soft-errors after driver 537.x upgrade causing degraded kernel fallback. Status: investigating with infra/vendor. Owner: Chen Wang.
- ISSUE-2029-120: small regression in top-1 output for int8 A/B rollout on summarization model (tracked in bench-quality). Mitigation: rollback int8 for model summarizer-v3 until additional calibration completed. Owner: Sofia Ortega.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

A. High tail-latency incident (p95/p99)
1. Triage: check metrics dashboard (dashboard: runtime/latency-overview) and identify affected models/tenants
2. Check recent deploys: git sha and infra change in last 6 hours
3. Run quick profile: curl -u admin:token "https://<runtime-node>/debug/profile?duration=30s&level=light" and fetch flame graph
4. If coalesce wait is high -> temporarily lower coalesce_window_ms for affected pool:
   - kubectl -n runtime set env deployment/runtime-svc COALESCE_WINDOW_MS=2 --record
5. If GPU memory pressure -> move affected tenants to dedicated-reserved pool via orch-svc API: POST /v1/pools/migrate {tenant_id, pool=reserved}
6. If kernel regression suspected -> rollback to previous runtime-svc image: kubectl rollout undo deployment/runtime-svc --to-revision=<rev>
7. Post-incident: create postmortem, capture profiles, and add to regression triage board

B. Model onboarding performance checklist
1. Run microbench on target hardware: tools/bench/run_microbench --model <model> --hw a100-40gb --batch 16 --seq 128
2. Capture profile and determine preferred kernel variant
3. Run quality checks with eval harness (pass threshold >= 98% for text-similarity baseline)
4. If quantized path used -> run 10k sample correctness checks and collect distribution drift metrics
5. Add model entry to model-catalog with kernel_hint, recommended_pool, and profiling artifacts link

C. Emergency rollback steps
1. Identify bad image sha: kubectl -n runtime get deployments runtime-svc -o yaml | grep image
2. Undo rollout: kubectl rollout undo deployment/runtime-svc --to-revision=<prev-rev>
3. Monitor p95/p99 and GPU util for 30m
4. If rollback fails -> scale down new nodes and scale up previous template nodes using infra autoscaler (contact eng-infra on-call)

8) Team wiki & onboarding links

Key pages and artifacts:
- Team wiki (living docs): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-team-wiki-playbook-2027-12-01
- Bench reports bucket: s3://redwood-bench-reports/
- Bench thresholds repo: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/tree/main/bench
- Debug endpoints catalog: internal runbook (link: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/debug-endpoints)
- On-call roster & runbook index: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks

New hire checklist (runtime-specific):
- Read: this playbook, runtime architecture reference, and kernel scheduling ADR
- Run: microbench locally and submit a bench result PR to get familiar with CI
- Shadow: two pager on-call with senior engineer for two weeks

Appendices

A. Common CLI snippets
- Collect a 60s profile from staging:
  curl -s -u admin:token "https://runtime-staging.internal/debug/profile?duration=60s&level=full" > /tmp/profile-$(date +%F).json
- Upload bench report:
  aws s3 cp ./bench-report.json s3://redwood-bench-reports/$(date +%F)/bench-report.json
- Trigger microbench in infra CI:
  gh workflow run benchmark.yml --ref main --json '{"target":"a100-40gb","suite":"micro"}'

B. Config reference (selected keys)
- COALESCE_WINDOW_MS: string (ms) — adaptive batching delay window; default 4
- MAX_BATCH_SIZE: int — upper cap of micro-batch size; default 64
- LATENCY_BUDGET_MS: int — per-request target; default 25 for interactive
- KERNEL_SELECTOR_MODE: enum ["safe","aggressive","canary"]

C. Contacts and rotation
- Runtime on-call: rotation in PagerDuty (schedule: runtime-primary)
- PagerDuty escalation: eng-sre -> eng-platform -> CTO

If you find gaps or contradictions in these procedures, file a doc update PR and ping the reviewers listed above. This page is the canonical operational guide for the Serving Runtime team.
